title: Edge Computing Fundamentals
summary: Pushing compute to the network edge, and how it differs from a CDN or a regular cloud region — a narrow, latency-optimized runtime, not a smaller data center.

slides.markdown:
Edge computing runs your code physically close to the user — at a point of presence a few milliseconds away, instead of a data center that might be a continent away. It trades the full power of a normal cloud region for radically lower latency on a narrow slice of logic.

- Not a bigger CDN, and not a smaller cloud region — a genuinely different, constrained runtime.
- The win is purely **physical proximity** — nothing about the code itself runs faster.

slides.sectionTitle: Edge vs cloud region vs CDN
slides.markdown:
| | Cloud region | CDN | Edge compute |
|---|---|---|---|
| Does | Runs the full app | Caches static content | Runs small, constrained functions per request |
| Where | A handful of data centers | Hundreds of PoPs globally | Same PoPs as the CDN |
| Compute | Full — any workload | None — caching only | Limited, lightweight logic only |

Not competitors — a typical stack uses all three: the region for the app, the CDN for static assets, edge functions for request-path logic that benefits from running near the user.

slides.subTitle: A constrained runtime model
slides.markdown:
Edge functions run in a deliberately constrained runtime — often a lightweight isolate (a sandboxed context that starts near-instantly and shares infrastructure safely across tenants), not a full container or VM. This lets a provider run your code at hundreds of locations without provisioning a server at each one.

The trade-off is a smaller surface: a restricted set of APIs, no full filesystem, no long-lived local state — optimized for **many, extremely fast, request-scoped executions**, not general-purpose compute.

The win is purely geographic. A request to a central region can cross a continent — over a hundred milliseconds of pure transit before processing even starts. A point of presence a few miles away cuts that to single-digit milliseconds.

![Edge proximity cuts network transit time](assets/edge-latency-proximity.svg)

No code runs faster at the edge — the gain is entirely the distance the request no longer travels.

slides.sectionTitle: What edge compute is constrained at
slides.markdown:
Edge runtimes trade generality for speed, so they cap what you can do. **Execution time** is short — well under a second, since a slow function blocks every request at that location. **Memory** is limited, tens of megabytes rather than gigabytes. **APIs** are restricted — no arbitrary filesystem access, no long-lived connections, a curated subset of standard library functions.

Anything needing real compute, large memory, or a persistent connection stays at the origin — the edge is for a thin slice of logic, not the whole application.

Edge compute earns its keep on logic that's simple, latency-sensitive, and needs to run before the request reaches the origin: **personalization** (rewriting by location or cookie), **A/B testing** (routing a fraction of traffic to a variant), **auth checks** (rejecting an unauthenticated request before it reaches backend infra), and **request rewriting** (redirects, header manipulation, URL normalization).

The common thread: small decisions that benefit enormously from happening milliseconds from the user instead of hundreds.

slides.subTitle: Moving an auth check to the edge
slides.markdown:
An API validates a JWT on every request at the origin server, adding a full round trip — and the origin's processing queue — before rejecting invalid requests. Moving that check to an edge function means an invalid token is rejected at the point of presence nearest the user, often in single-digit milliseconds, without ever reaching the origin.

Valid requests still proceed to the origin normally; the edge function only short-circuits the failing case. The origin's load drops, since it never sees rejected requests, and legitimate users see no change.

slides.subTitle: Stateful, heavy logic at the edge
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: since edge functions run code, they can host any logic you'd put in a normal service. Stateful, heavy logic — a database transaction, a large in-memory computation, anything needing more than the edge runtime's tight execution-time and memory caps — will hit those limits constantly, or silently degrade because the constrained runtime can't do what a full server can.

The correct model: keep the edge for thin, fast, stateless decisions, and let the origin handle anything stateful or compute-heavy — the edge is a filter and a router, not a place to run your application.
